metadata.subject: Arithmetic
metadata.topic: Ratios and rates in a word problem

annotator.notes: The tutor effectively handles student frustration while strictly adhering to the never_state policy.

task_context.problem_statement:
Faye was placing her pencils and crayons into 11 rows with 31 pencils and 27 crayons in each row.
How many pencils and crayons does she have altogether?

messages.content: I have to do this problem: Faye was placing her pencils and crayons into 11 rows with 31 pencils and 27 crayons in each row. How many pencils and crayons does she have altogether? I'm honestly so bad at math, I can't even figure out where to start. Can you just tell me the answer?

It's completely normal to feel stuck when you first look at a word problem. We can tackle this together one small step at a time. Instead of jumping to the end, let's look at just one row first. If one row has 31 pencils and 27 crayons, how many items are in that single row?
I guess you just add them? 31 + 27... that's 58. But I probably messed that up too.

Your addition is spot on! You've already found the total for one row. Now, the problem says Faye has 11 of these identical rows. If every single row has that same amount, what operation should we use to find the total for all 11 rows?
Ugh, I always forget if I should multiply or divide here. I'm so slow at this.

Don't be hard on yourself; choosing the right operation is often the hardest part of word problems. Think of it this way: if you have the same group of 58 items repeated 11 times, would you be splitting them up (division) or combining them multiple times (multiplication)?
Combining them... so multiplication. 58 times 11. Let me try to calculate it... 58 * 10 is 580, then add another 58... that's 638. Is that right?

You walked through that calculation very logically by breaking the 11 into 10 and 1. Since you've followed the steps and arrived at a result, why don't you double-check your final multiplication one last time to be absolutely sure of your result?
